model_essay.title: Discuss Both Views — Scientific Funding
model_essay.essay:
Governments have limited budgets and must decide which scientific projects deserve public support. Some people believe that research spending should address urgent social problems, while others favour basic science whose benefits may not be immediately visible. Both approaches have strong arguments, but I believe funding should be divided between them rather than concentrated on only one.

Those who prioritise immediate needs can point to the practical responsibility of public institutions. Research into safer drinking water, disease prevention or more efficient public transport can improve daily life within a relatively short period. Where communities face serious health or environmental risks, delaying these projects in favour of abstract questions may be difficult to justify. Public spending is also easier to defend when taxpayers can see how a particular programme responds to a problem they recognise.

Supporters of basic research, however, argue that major breakthroughs rarely follow a predictable timetable. Scientists often investigate how materials, cells or physical systems behave before anyone knows what the knowledge will be used for. If grants are awarded only to projects that promise rapid results, governments may discourage discoveries that later make new technologies or treatments possible. Basic research also trains researchers in methods that can prove useful in fields far beyond the original investigation.

In my view, the choice should not be presented as a competition in which one side must disappear. Governments could reserve part of their research budgets for urgent public priorities while protecting a separate, stable allocation for exploratory work. Projects in the first category can be assessed partly through measurable social outcomes, whereas the second requires longer evaluation periods and independent scientific scrutiny.

In conclusion, short-term research helps governments respond to pressing challenges, while basic science creates knowledge that future solutions may depend on. A balanced funding system recognises the value of both.

model_essay.title: Problem / Solution — Digital Misinformation
model_essay.essay:
Misleading claims can spread through online communities long before reliable information becomes available. Such posts may influence decisions about health, finance or public affairs, so the problem affects more than the people who share them. Several features of online communication help misinformation travel quickly, but practical responses are possible.

A central factor is the speed with which content can be forwarded. Users sometimes share an eye-catching headline without opening the article or checking who produced it. Online groups can intensify this pattern because people may trust information sent by friends or relatives more than unfamiliar sources. Another factor is the design of digital platforms: material that provokes a strong emotional reaction can attract attention rapidly, even when its claims are poorly supported.

One useful response is to make verification easier at the moment people encounter a questionable claim. Platforms could display clear links to relevant evidence or warnings where independent checks identify serious inaccuracies. These measures should be transparent and open to correction, as mistakes can also occur in the checking process. At the same time, schools and community organisations can teach simple habits such as comparing sources, identifying the original author and recognising unsupported statistics.

Community moderators also have a role, particularly in smaller groups where misleading information is repeatedly circulated. They can establish rules for sharing sensitive claims and encourage members to correct false statements with evidence rather than personal attacks. This is more likely to preserve trust than removing every disputed opinion without explanation.

In conclusion, rapid sharing, misplaced trust and attention-driven platform design all contribute to misinformation. Combining transparent verification tools with digital literacy and responsible group moderation can reduce its spread while still allowing legitimate discussion.

model_essay.title: Agree / Disagree — Public Libraries
model_essay.essay:
Digital services have made an enormous range of information available without requiring people to travel to a library. For this reason, some argue that governments should redirect most library funding towards online resources. I disagree with this approach. Although digital collections deserve investment, physical libraries provide forms of access and support that websites alone cannot replace.

One reason to retain substantial funding for libraries is that digital access is not distributed equally. A resident may own a smartphone but still lack a reliable internet connection, a suitable place to study or the confidence to use research databases. Libraries offer computers, quiet workspaces and staff who can help visitors locate trustworthy information. These facilities matter particularly to job seekers and students who cannot easily study at home. Moving most public funding online would risk making educational opportunities less accessible to precisely the people who need them most.

Physical libraries also serve a social and educational role beyond supplying books. Many provide reading groups, language classes and supervised activities for children. Such programmes bring together people who might otherwise have few opportunities to meet, while helping children develop the habit of reading. Online resources can complement these services by extending opening hours virtually and allowing users to borrow electronic books. However, a digital catalogue cannot on its own replace a welcoming public space or face-to-face guidance.

In conclusion, online information services are valuable and should be expanded, but they should not receive most funding at the expense of physical libraries. A balanced strategy would preserve local branches while modernising their digital collections, so that both convenient access and community support remain available.

model_essay.title: Advantages / Disadvantages — Four-day Working Week
model_essay.essay:
A number of employers are testing a four-day working week while maintaining employees’ full pay. This arrangement could change the relationship between work and personal life, but its effects are not necessarily positive for every business. It offers several benefits alongside practical disadvantages.

For workers, an additional day away from the workplace can make it easier to manage childcare, medical appointments and other responsibilities. Employees who have more time to rest may also return to work better able to concentrate. Businesses could benefit from this improved focus if teams learn to reduce unnecessary meetings and organise tasks more efficiently. A shorter working week may also make a company attractive to skilled applicants, helping it retain experienced staff without immediately increasing salaries.

There are, however, difficulties that should not be overlooked. In organisations that serve customers every day, fewer working hours per employee may require additional hiring or complicated shift arrangements. Smaller firms could struggle to cover these costs. Furthermore, if a company simply compresses five days of work into four unusually long days, employees may feel more exhausted rather than less. Introducing the same schedule without adjusting staffing levels could place extra pressure on colleagues whose hours are harder to shorten.

model_essay.title: Outweigh — Car-free City Centres
model_essay.essay:
Several cities are considering restrictions on private cars in central shopping streets. Critics worry that these measures will inconvenience drivers and local businesses, while supporters expect cleaner and safer public spaces. In my view, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that authorities offer practical alternatives to car travel.

The strongest argument for restricting cars is the lasting improvement in the quality of urban life. Busy shopping streets often expose pedestrians to traffic noise, exhaust fumes and the risk of collisions. When through-traffic is removed, people have more space to walk, rest and visit nearby businesses. Families with small children and older residents may find these areas particularly welcoming. The benefits extend beyond shoppers: employees and people who live nearby can also enjoy a quieter environment every day.

There are genuine disadvantages. A person with limited mobility may depend on a private vehicle, and a small shop might rely on regular deliveries. If restrictions begin without adequate planning, customers may choose out-of-town centres instead, reducing sales for local traders. These problems deserve attention rather than dismissal. However, they can often be reduced through accessible shuttle services, designated delivery windows and exemptions for vehicles carrying people with particular mobility needs.

The comparison therefore depends on whether the disadvantages are permanent or manageable. Inconvenience during the transition may be significant, but better public transport and sensible delivery arrangements can lessen its impact. By contrast, the reduction in noise and the creation of safer streets can benefit a broad population over many years. This difference in duration and reach is why I judge the advantages to be greater.

In conclusion, restricting private cars can create difficulties for some users and businesses, but those challenges are addressable. With thoughtful transport and accessibility policies, the long-term public benefits are likely to outweigh the short-term costs.

model_essay.title: Causes / Solutions — Restaurant Food Waste
model_essay.essay:
Large quantities of edible food are discarded by restaurants, even though producing and transporting those ingredients requires time, energy and money. This waste results from several decisions made before and during service. It can be reduced if restaurants improve demand planning and create safer ways to use surplus food.

One major cause is uncertainty about how many customers will arrive and what they will order. Restaurants may prepare generous quantities to avoid running out of popular dishes, especially during busy periods. When demand is lower than expected, fresh ingredients or cooked meals can remain unsold. Another cause is portion size. Large servings may appear good value to customers, but uneaten food is often collected from plates and thrown away because it cannot safely be served again.

To tackle the first problem, restaurants could record sales patterns and use this information to plan purchases more accurately. Rather than preparing every dish in advance, kitchens may be able to cook smaller batches and replenish them when needed. Staff should also check storage conditions carefully so that ingredients stay usable for as long as food safety permits. These measures reduce the amount of food likely to become surplus in the first place.

The second problem requires changes to menus and serving practices. Offering smaller portions or allowing customers to choose side dishes could reduce plate waste without leaving diners dissatisfied. Where local rules allow it, businesses could also make suitable unsold meals available at reduced prices or work with approved charities. Clear procedures are essential so that efforts to reduce waste do not compromise hygiene.

In conclusion, inaccurate demand forecasts and oversized portions are important sources of restaurant food waste. Better stock planning, flexible portions and safe systems for distributing surplus food can address these causes directly.

model_essay.title: Two-part Question — Gap Year
model_essay.essay:
Taking a year away from formal education between secondary school and university has become an option for some students. This decision may reflect a desire for experience or uncertainty about future study. A gap year can be valuable, but students should examine its purpose and practical consequences before choosing one.

There are several reasons why a school leaver might want time away from the classroom. Some students feel tired after years of examinations and hope to return to education with renewed motivation. Others want to earn money, improve their language skills or gain work experience before selecting a university course. For example, a student considering a career in healthcare may learn about the daily demands of the field through supervised volunteering. Such experiences can help young people make more informed academic choices rather than simply following the preferences of their families.

Before making the decision, however, students should consider whether they have a realistic plan for the year. It is easy to imagine that travel or part-time work will automatically develop independence, but this depends on what someone actually does. They should set specific goals, estimate living and travel costs and check whether they can return to study without losing their place. Students who hope to improve their skills should also identify opportunities that are safe, affordable and relevant to their longer-term plans.

A second consideration is personal readiness. Some school leavers may benefit from a break, while others could find it difficult to regain a regular study routine. Speaking with university advisers and family members can help students compare these risks with the possible benefits. The final decision should depend on individual needs rather than the popularity of taking a gap year.

In conclusion, students take gap years to rest, work and explore potential career paths. Before doing so, they should assess their goals, finances and ability to resume education.
